canonical_statement: The study compared ICU clinician and artificial-intelligence prediction performance for multiple patient outcomes in both retrospective and prospective settings.
The ABeICU database used for AI model development contained 55,689 ICU admissions from 48,672 de-identified adult patients across 15 Alberta ICUs between February 2012 and December 2019.

population.label: ABeICU ICU admissions used as the source cohort

canonical_statement: ABeICU model-development eligibility required adults aged 18 years or older with an ICU length of stay longer than 24 hours; patients with missing outcome labels were excluded for the corresponding outcome.

population.label: ABeICU model-development eligibility
inclusion_criteria: ICU length of stay longer than 24 hours
exclusion_criteria: Missing target label for the modeled outcome

canonical_statement: The retrospective clinician-versus-AI comparison used 990 ICU admissions from the reserved ABeICU test cohort after data-linkage issues reduced the intended 1,000-patient set.
After prospective clinician-prediction forms were linked to extracted ICU data, 238 ICU admissions from 215 patients remained for prospective clinician-versus-AI comparisons.

population.label: Prospective linked comparison cohort: 238 ICU admissions from 215 patients

canonical_statement: AI models were trained on 46,631 ICU admissions and the same selected models were used to generate AI predictions in both the retrospective and prospective comparisons.

The primary predicted outcomes were in-hospital mortality, 30-day post-discharge mortality, ICU length of stay, and hospital length of stay; secondary outcomes were delirium and acute kidney injury during the ICU stay.

Acute kidney injury was defined by KDIGO serum-creatinine criteria: an increase of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or at least 1.5 times baseline over the previous 7 days; at least two serum-creatinine measurements were required.

outcome.definition: KDIGO serum-creatinine criteria: increase >=0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or >=1.5 times baseline over 7 previous days

canonical_statement: Delirium was determined using the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist, with a score of 4 or greater indicating delirium.
Each AI model used patient data from the first 24 hours in the ICU to predict its target outcome at 24 hours after ICU admission.

For each classification outcome, the authors trained logistic-regression, support-vector-machine, XGBoost, random-forest, and neural-network models; for ICU and hospital length of stay, elastic net replaced logistic regression in the same five-model comparison.
Model hyperparameters were tuned with Bayesian optimization in Optuna, and best-model selection optimized median AUROC for classification and RMSE for regression in 5-fold cross-validation.
Classification output thresholds were optimized for F1 score in 5-fold cross-validation.
XGBoost was the best-performing model for every modeled outcome based on the prespecified median AUROC or RMSE selection criteria.
The four classification models were reported as reasonably calibrated on retrospective test data, with Brier scores ranging from 0.1145 to 0.1926.
The optimized classification thresholds were 0.45 for in-hospital mortality, 0.48 for 30-day mortality, 0.52 for acute kidney injury, and 0.50 for delirium.

Decision-curve analysis showed positive net benefit over treating all or none in all evaluated cases except prospective acute-kidney-injury prediction; optimized thresholds had positive net benefit except retrospective 30-day mortality and prospective acute-kidney-injury prediction.

Seven FMC ICU clinicians - three physicians (two intensivists and one fellow) and four ICU nurses - provided retrospective predictions for the 990 ABeICU test cases using de-identified first-24-hour patient data presented in REDCap.

Fifty retrospective cases were randomly selected for predictions by all seven clinicians; the remaining cases were divided into five sets of approximately 190 cases so that each patient had predictions from one, two, or seven clinicians.

Prospective bedside predictions were collected in a 28-bed tertiary FMC ICU from adult patients who had been in the ICU for 16-24 hours, with clinicians encouraged to use all information available in routine clinical practice.
The prospective collection obtained 465 clinician predictions for 287 patients from September 1, 2020 through December 31, 2022, with each patient predicted by one to four clinicians.

population.label: Prospective clinician-prediction collection: 465 predictions for 287 patients

canonical_statement: Prospective clinicians were grouped as subspecialized physicians (attending physicians and fellows), physicians in training (residents and interns), and nurses.

After prospective data linkage and exclusion of outcomes that were unascertainable or had already occurred in the first 24 hours, the number of predictions analyzed varied from 145 to 287 depending on the outcome.

Clinician-AI hybrid classification predictions used logical AND and OR operations, while hybrid regression predictions used averaging, minimum, or maximum; when multiple clinician predictions existed they were aggregated before combination with the AI prediction.

Clinician and AI performance metrics were compared with two-sample Wilcoxon rank-sum tests applied to 1,000 bootstrap samples of the test data, stratified by number of clinicians retrospectively and clinician type prospectively.

For classification outcomes, clinician 5-point Likert predictions were dichotomized by treating "most likely" and "likely" as positive; when multiple clinicians predicted the same patient, Likert responses were averaged before dichotomization.
Prediction-level inter-rater agreement was assessed with Cohen kappa for classification predictions and the intraclass correlation coefficient for regression predictions.

Retrospectively, AI generally outperformed clinicians on classification outcomes when predictions came from one or two clinicians, whereas aggregated predictions from seven clinicians tended to outperform AI for all classification outcomes except delirium.
In the retrospective two-clinician group, clinician in-hospital-mortality specificity was higher than AI specificity: median 0.925 (95% CI 0.895-0.953) versus 0.896 (95% CI 0.861-0.926), p<0.001.

population.label: Retrospective in-hospital mortality cases with two clinician predictions

concept.text: Aggregated predictions from two ICU clinicians

canonical_statement: In the retrospective one-clinician group, clinician acute-kidney-injury sensitivity was higher than AI sensitivity: median 0.652 (95% CI 0.564-0.738) versus 0.551 (95% CI 0.464-0.650), p<0.001.

population.label: Retrospective AKI cases with one clinician prediction

canonical_statement: In the retrospective two-clinician group, ICU length-of-stay MAE was lower for clinicians than for AI: median 4.436 days (95% CI 4.109-4.786) versus 4.534 days (95% CI 4.275-4.800), p<0.001.

ICU length-of-stay prediction mean absolute error

canonical_statement: In the retrospective two-clinician group, hospital length-of-stay MAE was lower for clinicians than for AI: median 16.73 days (95% CI 15.46-18.08) versus 17.14 days (95% CI 16.18-18.08), p<0.001.

canonical_statement: Both clinicians and AI had poor R-squared performance for retrospective ICU and hospital length-of-stay prediction, and the seven-clinician aggregation did not surpass AI for these regression outcomes.

Prospectively, subspecialized physicians generally outperformed AI on classification outcomes other than delirium; physicians in training and nurses tended to perform worse than subspecialized physicians.
For prospective in-hospital-mortality sensitivity, AI exceeded subspecialized physicians: clinician median 0.625 (95% CI 0.384-0.857) versus AI median 0.700 (95% CI 0.444-0.923), p<0.001.

population.label: Prospective in-hospital mortality cases predicted by subspecialized physicians

canonical_statement: For prospective delirium prediction, no performance metric differed significantly between subspecialized physicians and AI.

Physicians in training and nurses generally outperformed AI for prospective 30-day mortality on most performance metrics but were generally outperformed by AI for acute-kidney-injury and delirium prediction.
For prospective delirium specificity among nurses, clinicians exceeded AI: median 0.681 (95% CI 0.500-0.850) versus 0.640 (95% CI 0.444-0.826), p<0.001.

population.label: Prospective delirium cases predicted by nurses

canonical_statement: For prospective length-of-stay prediction, clinician types generally had lower MAE than AI, whereas AI generally had better RMSE and R-squared values.

For prospective hospital length-of-stay MAE in subspecialized physicians, AI had lower error: clinician median 42.646 days (95% CI 28.483-61.359) versus AI median 37.798 days (95% CI 25.583-54.494), p<0.001.

population.label: Prospective hospital LOS cases predicted by subspecialized physicians

concept.text: Hospital length-of-stay prediction mean absolute error

canonical_statement: For prospective ICU length-of-stay RMSE among physicians in training, trainees had lower error than AI: median 9.295 days (95% CI 5.087-13.839) versus 9.641 days (95% CI 6.108-14.277), p<0.001.

population.label: Prospective ICU LOS cases predicted by physicians in training

concept.text: ICU length-of-stay prediction root mean squared error

canonical_statement: For prospective ICU length-of-stay R-squared among physicians in training, trainees had higher R-squared than AI: median 0.022 (95% CI -0.520 to 0.317) versus -0.056 (95% CI -0.551 to 0.061), p<0.001.

canonical_statement: Hybrid clinician-AI classification generally produced the best metric values: AND combinations tended to maximize specificity and PPV, whereas OR combinations tended to maximize sensitivity and NPV.
The retrospective seven-clinician classification group was an exception to the hybrid advantage: aggregated clinician predictions performed as well as or better than the clinician-AI hybrids.

Hybrid regression approaches generally yielded the best MAE, RMSE, and R-squared performance, although AI alone was best in some comparisons and the best hybrid operator varied among averaging, minimum, and maximum.
Inter-rater agreement was generally poor among clinicians in both retrospective and prospective settings; clinician-AI agreement was mostly poor to fair, with moderate agreement in limited subgroups.

A sensitivity analysis that treated the middle Likert category as positive increased sensitivity and NPV at the expense of specificity and PPV, and the authors judged the primary Likert threshold to be the better choice.

The authors concluded that AI generally outperformed clinicians retrospectively, but aggregation of seven clinicians enabled clinicians to outperform AI; prospectively, subspecialized physicians outperformed AI except for delirium.
The authors concluded that clinicians and AI had complementary predictive strengths and that combined clinician-AI predictions would be preferable when both are available.
Approximately 35% of prospectively collected clinician predictions failed data linkage because of erroneous manual patient-identifier entry.

Prospective data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic while AI models had been trained on pre-COVID data, creating a plausible distribution shift that may have reduced prospective AI performance.
Only seven clinicians contributed to the retrospective comparison, limiting generalizability of the retrospective clinician benchmark.
The prospective clinician-type categories were broad and may not have fully captured differences in clinical experience, training, and professional role.
Prospective clinicians made predictions 16-24 hours after ICU admission, whereas the AI model could use all available data through 24 hours, creating an information-window imbalance.

Excluding patients from AKI and delirium analyses because required measurements were unavailable or the outcome had already occurred in the first 24 hours reduced sample size by approximately 40% and introduced selection bias.
The study was conducted in a single Canadian province, and the authors stated that external validation is warranted.

The study received University of Calgary Conjoint Health Research Ethics Board approval (REB19-2107); clinician participants provided informed consent and patient consent for the retrospective data pull was waived.
ABeICU data cannot be shared without permission from Alberta Health Services and Alberta Health; clinician predictions may be shared on reasonable request without corresponding patient data.
The authors reported that source code for data preprocessing, model training, and analyses is available in a GitHub repository.

The study was funded by the Cumming School of Medicine, the Libin Cardiovascular Institute at the University of Calgary, and an NSERC Discovery Grant (RGPIN-2021-02588); the funders reportedly had no role in the study.
Joon Lee reported being a co-founder and major shareholder of Symbiotic AI, Inc.; the other authors reported no competing interest.
